name: BPC-157

b.x: A 2025 systematic review by Vasireddi's group [1] screened 544 papers on BPC-157. Thirty-six met inclusion criteria. Thirty-five were preclinical studies. One was clinical. That ratio says a lot about where the science stands right now. The review's orthopaedic search ran through June 3, 2024, and kept studies of mechanism, musculoskeletal outcomes, metabolism and safety. FDA's July 2026 briefing searched every use and counted five small human studies, two known only from meeting abstracts. The BPC-157 peptide (Body Protection Compound-157) is a pentadecapeptide (15 amino acids) from a protective protein in human gastric juice. In animal and cell studies, it promotes tissue repair through angiogenesis (VEGF-driven blood vessel growth), nitric oxide modulation, and FAK-paxillin pathway activation in tendon cells. One property separates it from most peptides: it stays stable in human gastric juice [6]. In rats, oral dosing works for gut injuries; no human study has measured how much of an oral dose is absorbed. Animal data is reproducible across labs and species. Healing acceleration has been confirmed in tendons, ligaments, muscles, nerves, corneas, and intestinal ulcers. A 2024 intravesical case series (12 patients (n=12) with interstitial cystitis) reported 80 to 100 percent symptom resolution. A 2025 IV pilot by Lee and Burgess confirmed tolerability up to 20 mg intravenous in two adults. Community data adds a different kind of evidence. Across r/Peptides, ExcelMale, and Longecity, users have reported steady outcomes for years. Pain reduction and improved mobility within 1 to 3 weeks for soft tissue injuries. Gut symptom relief within days on oral dosing. Faster post-surgical recovery. The community figured out the standard protocol before the researchers caught up. 250 mcg subcutaneous twice daily, near the injury, for 4 to 6 weeks. BPC-157 has no FDA approval. The FDA placed it on the Category 2 bulk drug substance list in 2023, blocking compounding. Its nominators withdrew it, and FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists it as withdrawn. FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) discussed BPC-157 on July 23, 2026. No FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list, so compounding pharmacies cannot use it today. Compared to TB-500, BPC-157 targets local tissue repair near the injection site through angiogenesis and NO modulation. TB-500 works systemically regardless of injection location. The two are commonly paired in a 1:1 ratio for combined local and systemic coverage.

BPC-157 works through several repair pathways at once. That overlap is part of why it turns up across so many injury models. The primary mechanism is angiogenesis. BPC-157 upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), triggering new blood vessel formation at injury sites. More capillaries mean better oxygen and nutrient delivery to damaged tissue. This effect is documented across multiple independent labs. BPC-157 also modulates nitric oxide synthesis, shifting the NO system toward tissue protection. In the gut, this translates to mucosal repair and reversal of NSAID-induced damage. Sikiric and colleagues mapped this pathway extensively [2]. For tendons and ligaments, BPC-157 activates the FAK-paxillin signaling cascade. This pathway controls how cells attach to the extracellular matrix and migrate into damaged areas. That process is rate-limiting in tendon healing. In rats, BPC-157 interacts with dopamine systems [3] and shifts brain serotonin synthesis [5]. This dual modulation likely explains the neuroprotective effects in animal models and the neuropsychiatric side effects some users report at higher doses. Growth hormone receptor upregulation adds another layer. In rat tendon cells, BPC-157 appears to sensitize tissue to circulating growth hormone, which may contribute to the tissue remodeling users describe.
BPC-157 benefits center on tissue repair, gut healing, and neuroprotection across over 180 published studies and thousands of community reports.

Tendon and ligament healing in many animal models; in a 2026 rat Achilles trial [4], BPC-157 alone trended better without reaching significance. Community users consistently report functional improvement within 2 to 4 weeks of daily subcutaneous injection near the injury site.

Gut lining repair in rat models of NSAID damage, ulcers, and bowel injury. Community users with leaky gut or IBS symptoms on oral dosing (500 to 1,000 mcg fasted) often report relief within the first week.
Angiogenesis promotion through VEGF upregulation at injury sites in animal and cell studies. An independent Taiwanese lab tied it to VEGFR2 activation [7], not only the Sikiric group.

Neuroprotective effects in animal models of nerve crush, traumatic brain injury, and spinal cord damage. Community reports of faster nerve recovery after compression injuries match this preclinical data.
Stability in gastric juice is a rare trait for any peptide. Oral bioavailability has never been measured, but rat studies support an oral route for gut applications.
The Wolverine Stack (BPC-157 plus TB-500) is the most popular peptide combination in the community. It pairs local tissue repair with systemic healing support.

Scientific Evidence
Based on 22 key studies · Preclinical
Strong preclinical evidence across 180+ PubMed papers (tendons, ligaments, gut mucosa, nerves, muscle).

Human data is extremely limited: ~30 subjects across all published studies. 2025 systematic review (Vasireddi et al.) found 35 preclinical + 1 clinical study from 544 screened. 2025 IV pilot (Lee & Burgess, n=2) showed tolerability up to 20 mg IV. 2024 intravesical interstitial cystitis series (n=12, 80-100% symptom resolution). No completed Phase II/III trial. No published oral bioavailability data in humans.
Key Study

Vasireddi et al. 2025, "Emerging Use of BPC-157 in Orthopaedic Sports Medicine: A Systematic Review," HSS J. PMID 40756949 / PMC12313605: screened 544 papers, 36 met inclusion, 35 preclinical + 1 clinical; consistent positive musculoskeletal outcomes across animal models; authors recommend caution given evidence quality
Limitations

No completed Phase II/III human trials. FDA's 2026 review found five small human studies, about 80 people in all; the three published pilots cover about 30. About 75% of PubMed records for BPC-157 (175 of 233 on Oct 13, 2026) list Sikiric as an author: limited independent replication. No BPC-157 trial has posted results on ClinicalTrials.gov. The 2015 Phase I PCO-02 trial (NCT02637284) last reported "active, not recruiting" in December 2015. Oral bioavailability never quantified in humans. IM bioavailability: 14-19% (rats) vs 45-51% (dogs): human figure unknown. Long-term safety unknown. FDA Category 2 classification (2023-2026) cited immunogenicity risk and insufficient characterization of peptide impurities in compounded preparations. FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists BPC-157 as withdrawn by its nominators; PCAC discussed it on July 23, 2026.
Community Experience
The most widely discussed healing peptide online.
Community dosing: 250–500 mcg/day subcutaneous in 1-2 injections near injury; 500–1,000 mcg/day oral (fasted) for gut applications

Standard protocol (250 mcg 2x/day SC near injury) dominates community consensus. Most users report measurable improvement in soft tissue injuries within 1-3 weeks. Gut healing via oral route (500-1,000 mcg fasted) frequently reported effective within days to 2 weeks. Side effects are real but polarized: most tolerate it well at standard doses; a meaningful minority report anxiety, panic attacks, and mood changes, especially above 500 mcg/day or with SSRI/SNRI use.

Science and community agree on core healing mechanisms (angiogenesis, collagen synthesis, gut repair). Divergence: community doses (250-500 mcg/day) were never validated in a human dose-finding trial. Community widely reports neuropsychiatric side effects (anxiety, panic, anhedonia) that barely appear in preclinical literature: animal models cannot self-report mood effects. The modulation documented in rat studies of dopamine (PMID 9073154) and serotonin (PMID 15531385) provides plausible mechanistic basis for community-reported mood effects.

Alternative Routes
Subcutaneous (primary)
Reference route: no adjustment needed; community doses (250-500 mcg) are based on SC
Near-injury injection for local effects; abdomen for systemic/gut. Human SC bioavailability unknown; IM bioavailability in rats 14-19%, dogs 45-51%.
Intramuscular
Same dose as SC; IM Tmax was 3 min in rats and 6 to 9 min in dogs (He et al. 2022); the study did not test SC
Less community-preferred than SC: SC is equally effective and less painful. No evidence IM outperforms SC for injury healing outcomes.
Oral
Community doses 500-1,000 mcg/day oral vs. 250-500 mcg/day SC: higher dose compensates for unquantified oral bioavailability loss

BPC-157 is uniquely acid-stable among peptides: survives gastric transit. Oral bioavailability has never been quantified in humans or published animal PK studies. For gut healing, direct mucosal contact is part of the mechanism. For musculoskeletal injury, SC remains preferred.
Intravenous (IV)
2025 pilot: 10-20 mg IV in clinical setting: far above community SC doses; not applicable to self-use protocols

Lee & Burgess 2025 (PMID 40131143): n=2 healthy adults, up to 20 mg IV over 1 hour, no adverse events, no biomarker changes. Clinical-only route. Risk of infection, air embolism, and anaphylaxis precludes self-administration.
Works With

BPC-157 provides targeted local repair at the injury site; TB-500 acts systemically to reduce inflammation and drive cell migration body-wide. Together they cover local + systemic healing: the "Wolverine Stack." Most popular injury-recovery combination in the peptide community.
BPC-157 250-500 mcg/day SC near injury + TB-500 2.5 mg 2x/week SC anywhere. 4-8 weeks loading, then half-frequency maintenance.
GHK-Cu
GHK-Cu promotes collagen synthesis, skin healing, and anti-aging tissue remodeling. Stacked with BPC-157 to optimize quality of new collagen and reduce scarring during structural repair.
BPC-157 250 mcg 2x/day SC near injury + GHK-Cu 1-2 mg/day SC. GHK-Cu sometimes used topically at wound site alongside systemic BPC-157.
Ipamorelin

Ipamorelin pulses growth hormone, augmenting systemic anabolic and tissue repair capacity. Community rationale: BPC-157 targets the injury locally; ipamorelin elevates the GH environment for faster overall recovery. No human combination data exists.
BPC-157 250 mcg 2x/day SC + Ipamorelin 200-300 mcg SC 30-60 min pre-sleep.
Avoid
SSRIs / SNRIs (Sertraline, Escitalopram, Venlafaxine, Fluoxetine, etc.)

In rats, BPC-157 modulates dopamine pathways (PMID 9073154) and brain serotonin synthesis (PMID 15531385). Multiple community reports document worsened anxiety, agitation, and mood instability when combining with antidepressants. No human interaction study exists. Mechanistic basis is plausible; risk is not quantified.
Anticoagulants / Antiplatelets (Warfarin, Heparin, DOACs, high-dose Aspirin)
BPC-157 may modulate coagulation pathways (also listed under its drug interactions). Potential additive effect on bleeding risk with anticoagulants. No human evidence; precautionary.
Anti-VEGF Drugs (Bevacizumab / Avastin, Ranibizumab, Aflibercept)
Anti-VEGF drugs mechanistically oppose BPC-157's primary angiogenic action (VEGF upregulation). Combining is pharmacologically contradictory and would likely reduce therapeutic effect of both.

FDA's 2026 review counted five small human studies, about 80 people in all; the three published pilots cover about 30 of them. The published literature calls it well-tolerated. That is accurate for what it covers; it just does not cover much. At standard doses (250 to 500 mcg per day), most users report no problems. The side effect picture changes above 500 mcg per day and in people on SSRIs or SNRIs. Anxiety and panic attacks are the most commonly reported serious community side effects. In rats, BPC-157 interacts with dopamine and adrenergic systems (Sikiric and colleagues) [3] and shifts brain serotonin synthesis [5]. Users with pre-existing anxiety disorders and those on serotonergic medications report the highest rates of this effect. Heart palpitations show up repeatedly in community reports, typically in the first few days of a cycle. They tend to clear within a week. Mood changes, including anhedonia, irritability, and a vague sense of feeling "off," affect a subset of users. These track with the dopaminergic and serotonergic modulation in preclinical work. They are more common at higher doses. Insomnia and vivid dreams come up occasionally. Brain fog above 750 mcg per day appears in community reports with no preclinical correlate. Nausea is more frequent with oral dosing. Some users report zero effect. Product quality is the usual explanation. Finnrick Analytics tested 450 samples from 64 companies; purity ranged from 82 to 100 percent, with 8 percent of samples containing endotoxin contamination. Contraindications: pregnancy and breastfeeding (no reproductive data), active cancer or cancer history (angiogenesis could theoretically feed tumor growth), children under 18 (no pediatric data). The SSRI/SNRI interaction risk warrants a conversation with your prescriber.
Common Issues & Solutions
Anxiety or panic attacks: drop immediately to 250 mcg 1x/day; if symptoms persist beyond 48h, discontinue entirely. Do not increase dose later. If on SSRIs/SNRIs, treat as a contraindication.

Heart palpitations in first 3 days: usually transient; reduce dose and monitor. If palpitations persist beyond 3-4 days or are accompanied by chest tightness or dyspnea, discontinue and seek medical evaluation.

No effect after 2+ weeks: verify product purity via independent COA (mass spectrometry preferred); confirm reconstitution math; consider switching to SC injection if using oral for musculoskeletal injury; confirm injection is placed near the injury.

Injection site pain, swelling, or redness: rotate sites within the target area (1-2 inches). Use a fresh needle every injection. Confirm bac water and peptide are fully dissolved before drawing. Check needle gauge (29-31G recommended).
Worsening pain or stiffness in first 3-5 days: a transient pro-inflammatory healing response is plausible. Monitor closely; if it persists beyond day 5 or is severe, stop and reassess.

BPC-157: Product Quality high risk

Research-only market with no pharmaceutical manufacturing oversight. Compounding legally prohibited in the US (FDA Category 2 from 2023; listed as withdrawn by its nominators as of April 22, 2026; no 503A bulks rule since). All supply is research-grade product. Independent purity testing (Finnrick Analytics, 450 samples across 64 companies) found purity ranging from 82% to 100%: significant variability. FDA concerns on file include peptide impurities, inadequate characterization, and immunogenicity risk from inconsistent synthesis. Budget products carry the highest quality risk.
An independent COA carries more weight than an in-house test. Mass spectrometry confirmation of molecular weight is more reliable than HPLC purity alone.
Products without a third-party COA, or with peptide purity below 95%, carry the highest quality risk.
Zero-effect responses are frequently a product quality or underdosing problem, not a pharmacological failure: verify source before concluding BPC-157 doesn't work.

b.x: Source: Animal PK data only: after a single IV dose, t1/2 was 5.3 min in dogs and 15.2 min in rats; after IM dosing it stayed under 30 min (He et al., Front Pharmacol 2022, PMID 36588717; FDA July 2026 PCAC briefing). The chart shows the rat IV value. No study has measured how long its tissue effects last.

BPC-157 has no FDA approval for any indication. In the United States it is sold as a research chemical. FDA had placed it in 503A Category 2, its list of bulk drug substances that "may present significant safety risks." For BPC-157, FDA cites possible immunogenicity, peptide-related impurities and little or no safety data for the proposed routes. Its nominators withdrew it, and FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists it as withdrawn. PCAC discussed BPC-157 on July 23, 2026. No FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23). BPC-157 is prohibited by WADA under category S0, both in competition and out. Athletes subject to testing should not use it. Rules outside the US differ by country. In the US, BPC-157 is not on the DEA's list of controlled substances (August 2026). Product quality varies; a third-party certificate of analysis with mass spectrometry confirmation is the main record of what a batch contains. protocols.monitoringNotes: Zero human combination PK/PD data exists. All stack rationale is mechanistic inference from individual compound animal studies. WADA: both banned (BPC-157: S0, TB-500: S2.3). Baseline + 4-week CBC + metabolic panel recommended. Understand individual risk profiles of both compounds.

faqs.q: What is the recommended BPC-157 dosage?
faqs.a: These are community tiers, since no human dose-finding trial exists. Beginner: 250 mcg subcutaneous twice daily. Moderate: 500 mcg once daily. Aggressive: 500 mcg twice daily. Inject as close to the injury site as practical. A typical healing course runs 4-6 weeks. Community experience across thousands of reports consistently supports the 250-500 mcg/day range for soft tissue injuries.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of BPC-157?
faqs.a: The three published human reports (about 30 people) recorded no adverse effects (PMID 40789979), but none was built to detect rare problems. Community reports (thousands of users) most often mention anxiety or panic and palpitations in the first days of a cycle. Mood changes, insomnia, and nausea with oral dosing also come up. These are more common above 500 mcg per day and with SSRIs or SNRIs. The main concern is the limited human safety data.

BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid fragment of the human gastric protein Body Protection Compound. In animal and cell studies, it raises VEGF signaling, promotes angiogenesis at injury sites, and modulates nitric oxide pathways (PMID 22950504). Animal studies show accelerated healing in tendons, ligaments, muscles, and GI tissue. The mechanism involves multiple overlapping repair cascades rather than a single receptor target.

No. BPC-157 has preclinical status only. In the 2025 Vasireddi systematic review (PMID 40756949), 35 of the 36 included studies were preclinical. The one clinical study was a small retrospective knee-pain report. No completed Phase 1 or Phase 2 human trial has been published. BPC-157 was on the FDA Category 2 bulk drug substance list from 2023 until its nominators withdrew it; FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists it as withdrawn. PCAC discussed it on July 23, 2026. No FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list, so compounding pharmacies cannot use it today.

Add 2 mL bacteriostatic water to a 5 mg vial. That gives 2,500 mcg/mL, or 25 mcg per unit on a 100-unit insulin syringe. For 250 mcg, draw 10 units. For 500 mcg, draw 20 units. Swirl gently, don't shake. Store refrigerated at 2-8 degrees C and use within 4 weeks.

BPC-157 sits at a C on the Peptide Schedule safety scale, and the honest limitation is how little human data exists. FDA's 2026 review counted about 80 people across five small human studies, about 30 of them in published pilots. Community reports most often flag anxiety, panic attacks, and mood changes, especially above 500 mcg per day or alongside SSRIs and SNRIs, consistent with its documented dopamine and adrenergic modulation (PMID 9073154). Active cancer and pregnancy are contraindications.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of BPC-157?
faqs.a: The half-life of BPC-157 is 15.2 min IV in rats, 5.3 min in dogs; under 30 min after IM; no human data. This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: Over 220 PubMed papers and years of community reports, but only about 80 people across five small human studies. The BPC-157 peptide (Body Protection Compound-157) is a 15-amino-acid pentadecapeptide from human gastric juice. It has become the most discussed healing peptide online, with reliable community reports of accelerated tendon, ligament, and gut repair. Animal research backs the mechanism. The standard protocol (250 mcg subcutaneous twice daily near the injury) has been stable for years. Community evidence is strong; formal clinical proof is still catching up fast.
